html:
Tiwanaku was a powerful Andean society based near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca, in what is now western Bolivia, from about 500 to about 1000 CE. Its capital, also called Tiwanaku, stood at nearly 3,850 metres, one of the highest cities ever built.

The capital was a ceremonial centre of platforms, sunken courts and gateways of finely cut stone, such as the Gateway of the Sun with its carved staff god. The same staff god appears in the art of Wari, its contemporary to the north, and the two shared a religious imagery though they were separate powers.

Its food came from raised fields: strips of earth built up between water channels on the lakeshore. The water stored the day's heat and protected crops from frost at this altitude. Herds of llamas and alpacas carried goods across the high plain, and Tiwanaku colonies reached into the valleys of southern Peru and northern Chile.

What kind of state it was is debated. It was once seen as a military empire, but there are no forts, no clear royal tombs and no state roads. Many now see it as a network of powerful lineages bound by feasts and shared religion.

Tiwanaku declined around 1000 to 1100, during a long drought that would have ruined the raised fields. Its ruins were already ancient and sacred when the Inca arrived, and the Inca told stories placing the creation of the world at Lake Titicaca.
